vignette:
From across the operating table, the anesthesiologist’s voice cuts through the steady beep of the monitors. “Pressure’s dropping. We need to move.” The patient is a young man, maybe twenty-two, a deep laceration across his abdomen from a car accident. I clamp the bleeder, and for a second my hands freeze. The smell of cauterized tissue hits me—metallic, sharp, the same smell that hung in the air that night.

It was four years ago, during my final year of surgical residency, when I was deployed with a forward surgical team. We were in a makeshift tent, not even a proper hospital, somewhere in the Sahel. The convoy had been hit by an IED. The first casualty was a soldier, maybe nineteen, his legs shredded. I worked for two hours to save him. I remember the pressure of my gloves against torn muscle, the warmth of blood pooling around my fingers. I remember the dust kicking up every time a helicopter landed. I remember the screaming. Not just his—mine, inside my head, though I never let it out. We lost him on the table. The team leader told me it wasn’t my fault. I nodded. But I didn’t believe it.

Now, back in a civilian trauma center, I still don’t believe it.

Every time a young male patient comes in with a lower-body injury, my stomach knots. My palms sweat inside the sterile gloves. I double-check every clamp, every suture, as if my hesitation could cost another life. The attending here, Dr. Marcorian, says I’m “painfully meticulous.” He doesn’t know that I am trying to outrun the ghost of the soldier I couldn’t save.

I avoid the ambulance bay. The sound of sirens—especially the wailing European model they use here—is the same as the military convoy alarms. I take the stairs to the OR instead of the elevator, because the elevator doors sliding shut feel too much like a helicopter bay door closing on a body bag. I stopped eating lunch in the hospital cafeteria after a colleague reheated a container of stewed meat. The scent of cooked blood, even by proxy, made me gag and excuse myself to the restroom, where I sat on the floor for ten minutes, staring at the grout lines.

My hands are steady in surgery; they have to be. But the moment I leave the OR, they tremble. I wake up three or four times a night, drenched in sweat, convinced I hear the thud of mortars. My apartment is on the fifth floor. I sleep with the window open, even in winter, because I need to feel air on my face. I have not been on a date in two years. The last man I tried to see—a radiologist—I left mid-dinner because a car backfired outside the restaurant and I dropped my fork. He thought I was rude. He didn’t understand that for a second I was back in that tent, my gloved hands slick, the soldier’s eyes wide and blank.

I know the memories don’t match the present. I know the patient on the table today is a civilian, his wound clean, his chances good. But when the anesthesiologist says “pressure’s dropping,” my chest tightens, my vision tunnels, and I have to count backward from ten under my breath to keep from freezing. I don’t tell anyone. I can’t. Surgeons don’t freeze. Surgeons don’t cry in supply closets between cases. Surgeons don’t flinch when a nurse drops a metal tray.

But I do. I flinch. And then I pretend to cough, pretend to adjust my mask, and I keep cutting, keep stitching, keep saving lives that I am terrified of losing again.
